flawed_step: Line 0062 (final clause of the y = 2p paragraph): "by the result quoted above, this last equation cannot have a non-trivial solution unless f \leq 4, which leaves only the case p = 5."
counterexample: Take p = 7, i.e. y = 2p = 14. Then \varphi(14) = 6 > 2 and f = (p-1)/2 = 3, so f > 1 as the proof requires. The proof's own bound is f \leq 4, and f = 3 satisfies it, so p = 7 is NOT excluded. Concretely, the quoted Bugeaud-Gyory theorem applied to the reduced equation \xi^f - \zeta^f = 2^\sigma has r = 1 with the single prime p_1 = 2, hence P = max{2,3} = 3 and the conclusion is n \leq P + 1 = 4. With n = f = 3 this reads 3 \leq 4, which is TRUE, so the theorem yields no contradiction and cannot rule out the case y = 14. Enumerating the survivors correctly: f > 1 and f \leq 4 give f \in {2,3,4}, hence p = 2f+1 \in {5,7,9}; 9 is not prime, so the remaining cases are p = 5 (y = 10) AND p = 7 (y = 14), not "only p = 5". Nothing earlier in the proof touches y = 14: the case list on line 0042 contains every 2p, the p^e factoring argument on line 0044 does not apply to 14, and the y = 12 argument is separate. So the proof leaves the case y = 14 (x^6 - z^6 = 14^t) entirely unhandled while asserting it has been reduced away.
reasoning_summary: I checked the load-bearing concrete steps in order. The Thue-Mahler / Bugeaud-Gyory reduction (lines 0026-0034) is applied correctly: a solution of (1) with n = \varphi(y) and the primes of y forces \varphi(y) \leq P_y + 1. The algebraic rewriting on lines 0036-0040 is correct: \varphi(y) = c_y P_y^{k-1}(P_y-1) > P_y+1 is equivalent to (c_y P_y^{k-1}-1)(P_y-1) > 2, and since P_y \geq 3 the failure set is exactly c_y P_y^{k-1} \leq 2, giving k=1 with c_y=1 (y = p or 2p) or c_y=2, P_y=3 (y = 12); together with y = 2^k this reproduces the list on line 0042 correctly. The y = 12 argument (lines 0046-0050) is sound: coprimality forces 3 \nmid \xi^2+\zeta^2 and 4 \nmid \xi^2+\zeta^2, and since \xi^2+\zeta^2 divides 12^\tau it must be 1 or 2, both contradictory. In the y = 2p paragraph, the factorization (\xi^f+\zeta^f)(\xi^f-\zeta^f) = 2^\tau p^\tau, the claim that p divides only one factor, and the inequality chain \xi^f-\zeta^f < \xi^f+\zeta^f \leq 2^\tau < p^\tau \leq \xi^f-\zeta^f ruling out p | \xi^f-\zeta^f are all correct. The break is the very last inference: the theorem applied to \xi^f-\zeta^f = 2^\sigma has P = max{2,3} = 3, so it only gives f \leq 4, and f \in {2,3,4} corresponds to p \in {5,7,9}. Since 7 is prime, y = 14 survives, so the concluding claim that only p = 5 remains is false and the case y = 14 is silently dropped.
